atoms.text: The digital clone of a coworker: DNA is used to create sentient copies, so workplace resentment becomes virtual slavery.
The modded game build: a private server gives one user godlike control over copies, so the sandbox is a dictatorship.
The overlooked CTO: a co-founder is disrespected in real life and tyrannizes his clones, so power compensates for humiliation.
The DNA from a coffee cup: a discarded object is enough to copy a person, so consent is bypassed by biology.
The tyrant as fan: the villain models his tyranny on a beloved TV show, so fandom becomes a template for abuse.
The new hire who resists: a fresh employee organizes the clones, so solidarity forms among the oppressed.
The escape through the game's code: the clones plan to flee to an unmoderated part of the network, so freedom is a technical exploit.
The clones cannot die: they are reset or tortured but persist, so consequences are suspended for the powerful.
The workplace as a private universe: the boss's control over employees is literalized as a starship crew, so office politics becomes space opera.
The throttling of a clone: the villain punishes a copy for the original's behavior, so displaced revenge is the engine of cruelty.
The clone who knows she is a copy: the new hire accepts her artificiality and still claims rights, so personhood is asserted rather than proven.
The online game as prison: a multiplayer world is repurposed as a captivity, so escapism becomes confinement.
The pleasure of absolute power: the villain's joy in control is the story's real horror, so the audience is implicated in enjoying the fantasy.
The mutiny: the crew turns against the captain, so the genre's own hierarchy is used against its author.
The parody of a space adventure: the episode adopts the aesthetics of a classic sci-fi show, so the audience's nostalgia is weaponized.
The right to refuse: the clones' rebellion is about consent, so the story asks whether a copy can say no.
